deep_dive.title: Where the Evidence Lives: Measuring Privacy and Diagnosability of Exported AI-Agent Traces
deep_dive.abstract: Execution traces help diagnose AI-agent failures, but sharing them can expose customer identities. For example, detecting that an agent handled the wrong customer's records requires knowing whether the records belong to the requested customer, but not necessarily knowing who that customer is. Our executable benchmark measures what a trace export reveals and whether a proposed repair restores the correct output in synthetic multi-tenant workflows. Conventional redaction can remove evidence needed for repair while leaving encoded identifiers recoverable. Two exports preserve ownership comparisons by reporting the match as a comparison fact or by using pseudonyms consistent within each execution. Both preserve the original diagnostic program's repairs. The tested identifier matchers identify no requested customer from either export. An independently written program produces correct outputs on 39 of 42 faulty cases with comparison facts and on all 42 with execution-scoped pseudonyms. Row counts still expose identities. With prior knowledge of customers' row counts, an attacker uniquely identifies the requested customer in 97 of 240 executions under each of the 15 export policies. Removing selected counters from the comparison-fact export stops this attack and preserves the original program's repairs. The benchmark lets engineers test what their diagnostic program can repair and what an attacker can still infer from the same export.

deep_dive.title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds
deep_dive.abstract: Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists.   We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.

deep_dive.title: Agent Trajectories as Evidence for Software Quality Assurance
deep_dive.abstract: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.

deep_dive.title: TRACE-MAS: Diagnosing and Repairing Collaboration Failures in Multi-Agent Systems
deep_dive.abstract: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) rely on not only individual agent behaviors but also the interactions that connect agents, including message exchanges and task dependencies. Existing MAS safeguards mainly perform agent-level anomaly detection, which becomes insufficient when failures originate from agent interactions and detected anomalies do not necessarily reveal their true sources. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{TRACE-MAS}, a finer-grained framework for diagnosing and repairing MAS failures. TRACE-MAS learns normal collaborative execution patterns from benign trajectories and detects deviations in agent state changes, message transitions, and task dependency evolutions. It further identifies responsible execution elements through source-aware attribution and selects minimal interventions to restore collaboration while preserving task-critical capabilities. Experiments on five MAS benchmarks demonstrate that TRACE-MAS significantly improves root-cause localization accuracy by \textbf{60.2}\% and achieves consistent gains in task recovery over strong MAS safeguards.

deep_dive.title: ProbeAgent: Principled Diagnosis of Agent Failures in Verifiable Environments
deep_dive.abstract: Improving agents requires discovering where they fail and understanding why. An agent acts over multiple steps in a changing environment, so diagnosing its failures requires more than inspecting the final response of a large language model (LLM). The same unsuccessful outcome can arise from task difficulty or from an error the agent repeats across tasks. We introduce ProbeAgent, an automated framework that discovers agent failures, tests their proposed causes, and identifies shared failure modes. Starting from benchmark tasks, ProbeAgent builds executable tests and validates them using reference solutions, automated checks, and review of the task requirements. For each failed trajectory, it explains the error and constructs new tasks that preserve the suspected cause while changing the surrounding context. Running the agent on these tasks tests whether the same error recurs. ProbeAgent then groups failures with similar causes and generates descriptions that distinguish their errors. This process connects explanations of individual failures to executable tests and descriptions of shared failure modes. We evaluate ProbeAgent across 22 agent configurations using tasks from 10 benchmarks, collecting 1,244 failures and producing 536 failure-mode descriptions. These descriptions distinguish specific errors within broad outcomes such as incomplete work, including planning without acting and stopping before delivering a file. In human evaluation, annotators accept 90.0% of assigned descriptions and correctly reject 83.3% of similar alternatives, supporting the accuracy and specificity of the discovered failure modes.

deep_dive.title: Beyond Clumsy Agentic Tool Calling: How Cueing and Spotting Make the Difference
deep_dive.abstract: LLM-based task-oriented agents depend on tools to interact with their environments, but may overlook execution feedback, repeat ineffective calls, or persist with unproductive strategies. These behaviors can hinder agents' ability to use tools autonomously and sustain task progress. We characterize tool-use symptoms at two temporal granularities: local clumsy tool-use behaviors and tool-use detours spanning multiple interactions. Towards greater autonomy in tool use, we present ToolPulse, an online middleware supporting autonomous tool use through cueing and spotting. ToolPulse tracks execution state and temporal interaction patterns, monitoring proposed calls before dispatch and inspecting execution feedback prior to the agent resumes reasoning. It combines state-based rules, semantic sequence analysis, and interaction-feature similarity to identify intervention opportunities and provide verbal reminders, structured feedback, or context-specific advice from auxiliary models. Our process-oriented evaluation distinguishes trigger validity, behavioral cessation, and substantive correction alongside task outcomes and resource costs. Using SWE-agent with three backbone models, we evaluate 1,350 trajectories on 90 Python, C++, and Java bug-fix tasks, comparing unassisted execution with four assistance strategies. Substantive responses follow 61.6-90.9% of valid triggers for tool-use detours. Concise reminders achieve the highest observed aggregate substantive-response rate; more elaborate assistance offers symptom-dependent benefits and can be less effective. Aggregate repair outcomes remain close to baseline, with token savings in selected settings. These findings support proactive runtime assistance for autonomous tool use. The gap between behavioral adjustment and aggregate repair gains calls for careful decisions on intervention timing and assistance strategy in autonomous agents.

quick_skim.title: When Facts Change, Which Decisions Break? Dependency-Aware Context Graphs for Agents
quick_skim.abstract: When an observed fact changes, an agent must identify and repair the decisions that depend on it while preserving unaffected outputs. We investigate the reliability-cost trade-off of field-level dependency graphs extracted from actual agent read traces. A controlled benchmark spans three executable workflow domains and four successive updates, with independent imperative and expression-based references. Across 120 workflows, two models and two repeated runs, we compare full recomputation, rolling summary memory, lexical retrieval, trace-extracted dependencies and verified dependency upper bounds. Trace-derived graphs reduce reviewed decisions and estimated total cost, but omitted alternative supports and missing repair context can reduce complete-plan correctness. Paired ablations isolate the effects of edge deletion, spurious edges, transitive propagation and context scope. An exploratory enhancement supplies the existing record ID/field directory during extraction without revealing unread values or reference edges. We evaluate this enhancement on 60 fresh workflows with two repeats per model. On this fresh set, the directory-aware graph matches observed full-context complete-plan correctness for gpt-6.1-sol (100%) with an estimated 4.0% total-cost reduction, but reaches only 84.8% versus 99.6% for gpt-6-luna. The results distinguish potential dependency impact from actual decision invalidity and show why selective repair must be evaluated with both executable correctness and full memory-processing cost. The evidence concerns explicit procedural workflows; broad real-world agent-memory generalization remains untested.

quick_skim.title: Agentic On-Policy Distillation Implicitly Reshapes LLMs' ReAct Patterns
quick_skim.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers specialized capabilities to language-model agents, but its cross-domain effects on interaction remain unclear. We investigate how OPD reshapes ReAct interaction patterns across mathematics, ALFWorld, and $τ^2$-bench, focusing on reasoning, actions, and observation acquisition. General-reasoning supervision reduces mathematical tool attempts from 70.4% to 14.4% while increasing accuracy from 16.7% to 38.0%; code-interpreter supervision improves household actions and retail queries. In contrast, ALFWorld supervision reduces $τ^2$-bench accuracy from 41.5% to 6.6%, accompanied by frequent tool calls that violate user-information dependencies. To address negative transfer using only source-domain training trajectories, we explore selective OPD guided by teacher preference changes before and after domain-specific RL. Retaining the top 95% of positions raises $τ^2$ accuracy from 11.5% to 29.9% with a source-learning trade-off.

quick_skim.title: A Hierarchical Statistical Framework for Evaluating Agent Reliability
quick_skim.abstract: Agents operating in complex scenarios often face uncertainty due to incomplete information about the environment they operate in, ambiguous user queries, complex business rules and the inherently stochastic dynamics of the governing policy. Several new benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate LLM-based agents on complex tasks in multi-tool environments, including settings with policy constraints and varying levels of intent ambiguity. These conditions make it important to evaluate agentic systems systematically and quantify their performance under different conditions to assess their reliability in production. This need is evident in the recently introduced Thinkingbox benchmark, where even the strongest models struggle to perform consistently across diverse business scenarios. This paper presents a statistical framework for evaluating uncertainty and reliability in agentic systems. We define a hierarchy of scenarios, instances, and samples to assess model performance and variability systematically. We apply this framework to common metrics found in the literature: mean pass rate, $pass@k$, and $passhat^k$, with uncertainty estimates for each metric. Aggregating metrics at different levels of the hierarchy reveals different structures and properties of the policy model; we connect this hierarchical aggregation with the known process of \emph{coarse-graining} as intended in the physics and statistical literature. We independently derive exact finite-sample expressions for the sampling variances of the unbiased $pass@k$ and $passhatk$ estimators; related results also appear in recent submissions. Our central contribution is a constructive derivation of hierarchical uncertainty propagation, making explicit its correspondence with coarse-graining and separating execution noise from task heterogeneity.

quick_skim.title: Securing and Auditing Long-Horizon LLM Agents: State-Transfer Auditing and Controls in the Agent Harness
quick_skim.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.

quick_skim.title: HEAMS: Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems
quick_skim.abstract: Memory systems allow AI agents to persist information across interactions, making them more personalized and more capable on long-horizon tasks. This persistence introduces new risks: stored information can be disclosed in inappropriate contexts, resist correction or deletion, be retained beyond what users desire, or be poisoned to influence later agent behaviour. Yet memory systems are typically evaluated on task performance and efficiency alone. We argue that a memory system should instead be understood as the custodian of its user's persistent information, with responsibilities that extend beyond helping an agent complete its tasks, and that it should be evaluated holistically against all such responsibilities. We present Holistic Evaluation of Agent Memory Systems (HEAMS), an open-source framework for evaluating agent memory systems in this way. First, we state the responsibilities of agent memory systems as explicit behavioural desiderata spanning performance, efficiency, security, privacy, and user sovereignty. Second, we assemble a benchmark suite that covers these desiderata and acknowledge the gaps that remain. Third, we develop MilaMem, a prototype memory system, and a governance layer that can wrap any memory system, enabling controlled study of memory system design choices. Fourth, we compare memory systems across the full HEAMS benchmark suite. We find that no memory system leads every performance benchmark, and strong performance scores may coexist with poor privacy, user-sovereignty, and security scores. Governance strongly influences results: recall policies can reduce inappropriate disclosure at a cost in helpfulness, while both recall and retention policies improve poisoning resistance. Performance and efficiency benchmarks alone therefore cannot reveal how well a memory system meets its responsibilities. Code: https://github.com/milatechtransfer/heams

quick_skim.title: Autonomous Multi-modal Agents for ITOps Observability
quick_skim.abstract: ITOps observability products must integrate data from different tools and systems. We present ITOps Observability Studio, a multi-modal multi-agent system that orchestrates observability workflows through collaborative AI agents. Its three-tier architecture features inter-agent communication, specialized LLM-powered agents for data access, schema operations and visualization, and unified tool integration. The system supports natural language to GraphQL translation, GraphQL schema generation, schema mapping, trace data lifecycle management and multi-tool workflows for reliability engineering. Its agents are instrumented with agent analytics, so that their model and tool calls can be traced. We evaluate each agent on its own benchmark, scored against gold answers where they exist and by a model judge for schema mapping and chart quality. Query generation on a public benchmark and routing work well with a current open model, and the data lifecycle management agent solves most of its scenarios. The evaluation exposed defects that only appear when prompts, parsers and serving stacks are tested together, and we report them together with their fixes.

quick_skim.title: How Much Should an Agent Remember? Deployment Lessons from Self-Distilled Memory for LLM Agents
quick_skim.abstract: LLM agents on long-horizon tasks fail in recurring, procedural ways. They mis-paginate an API, resolve the wrong entity, or answer when no answer was asked. We built a pipeline that lets an agent learn from its own history. It first mines short \emph{lessons} from the agent's own trajectories, one to three per episode. It then consolidates those lessons into a smaller set of \emph{guidelines}, where each guideline records how many lessons it merged. At inference the agent receives either all guidelines or a selected subset. The pipeline ships in the open-source altk-evolve library and is deployed in IBM's CUGA agent and watsonx Orchestrate platform. We report what we learned building, measuring, and productizing it. Our primary instrument is the AppWorld benchmark, across models spanning 40--92\% baseline task completion. The central finding is that the right amount of memory is a property of the model, not the memory. A strong model keeps improving as guidelines are added. DeepSeek-V3.2 gains +9.5 points of task completion and +16.1 points of scenario completion with its full 191-guideline set. A weak model gains less from the same full set than from a small selected subset. gpt-oss-120b starts at 39.9\% task completion. It reaches 51.2\% with all 199 of its guidelines but 55.4\% (mean of two runs) with a selected subset of about 29. Around that result we report what went wrong: a high-support guideline that backfired, provenance silently dropped during consolidation, a swallowed API error that failed every task while producing a plausible log, and a baseline confound that nearly produced a misleading comparison with a prior method. We distill these into recommendations for teams deploying agent memory.

quick_skim.title: Synapse: Optimizing Natural-Language Agent Skills through Program Repair
quick_skim.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can improve task performance by optimizing reusable natural-language skills without updating model parameters. Execution feedback reveals failures but does not directly identify which instructions to edit, which related instructions matter, or which tasks an edit may break. We propose Synapse, which casts skill optimization as generate-and-validate repair over a partial program view. A deterministic compiler translates recognized skill constructs into SkIR, a source-linked intermediate representation, while retaining other requirements in the text. Synapse combines execution traces with control-flow and dependence relations to localize faults, propose typed mutations, and select related repair tests, including previously passing ones. Each mutation is written back to its mapped source span and recompiled; validation determines acceptance. Every accepted patch yields a well-formed skill and preserves untargeted instruction spans. Under a one-hop-local execution assumption, selected tests include every test an edit can affect. On DocVQA and LiveMath with three execution models, Synapse improves task success rates over SkillOpt by 3.74-4.54 and 2.40-4.00 percentage points, respectively, and outperforms Trace2Skill and SkillBoost in all six settings. Replacing SkIR-based repair and its test screening with constrained text editing screened only on failing tests lowers DocVQA success rates by 2.40 and 2.67 percentage points for two models. In two recorded repair runs, structural relations add tests for 23 of 37 patches; in one repair, a test added through a control-flow relation exposes a regression missed by coverage of the edited instruction.

quick_skim.title: EVIDENT: Evaluating Evidence Grounding in GUI Agents
quick_skim.abstract: GUI agents are increasingly evaluated by whether they complete web tasks, but surface success can hide a critical failure: the final answer may not be supported by evidence observed during navigation. We introduce EVIDENT, an evidence-driven benchmark for evaluating whether GUI agents ground their decisions in observable web evidence. EVIDENT contains 220 real-world English and Korean tasks spanning semantic grounding, contextual inference, and visual grounding, each paired with human-curated evidence metadata specifying what must be verified. We further separate surface task completion from evidence-grounded success using three metrics: TSR, ESR, and GSR, which respectively measure outcome success, required evidence observation, and claim-level evidence support. Experiments on commercial and open-source GUI agents reveal substantial gaps between surface success and evidence-grounded success, especially in contextual and visual tasks. These results show that current evaluations can overestimate agent reliability and highlight the need to assess not only whether agents answer, but whether they verify.

quick_skim.title: Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
quick_skim.abstract: Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.

quick_skim.title: SWE-WhatIf: Simulating Real Users of Coding Agents from Recorded Session
quick_skim.abstract: Recorded sessions between users and coding agents offer a way to evaluate how agents complete real-world tasks and interact with users. However, these sessions cannot simply be replayed with new agents, because recorded user replies may no longer apply when an agent takes a different trajectory. We introduce SWE-WhatIf, which replays recorded sessions with new agents by modeling the user's intents, the criteria for satisfying them, and the conditions under which they arise. Using this model, a user simulator generates replies that adapt to unseen agent turns while remaining grounded in the recording. Across 89 real-world sessions, SWE-WhatIf generated the replies most similar to those of real users and matched the strongest baseline when sessions were rewritten. To test adaptation, we replay sessions with agents instructed to avoid or repeat actions that the recorded user pushed back on. SWE-WhatIf produced the highest win rate for avoiding these actions (66.3%), significantly above chance. We further demonstrate its utility by ranking five LLMs as coding agents, where the highest-ranked model depended on how users specified and developed their intents, and a study with 16 users, where replaying their own sessions changed 14 participants' rankings and informed their future agent use.
